role.q: A campaign’s cost per lead doubled last week. How do you find out why?
role.why: The core performance question: a method, not a guess.
role.model: First check the data itself: tracking, a broken tag or form, a change in attribution or a reporting delay. Then split the cost per lead into its parts: cost per click (auction, bids, competition) and conversion rate (landing page, offer, audience). Break it down by channel, campaign, device and audience to find where the change comes from, and line it up with what changed: a new ad, a budget move, a site release. Fix the cause, then explain the impact and what you will monitor.

role.q: How would you build the SEO plan for a new website?
role.why: Tests whether you know SEO is technical, content and authority, in that order of priority.
role.model: Start with the business goal and the audience, then keyword research: what people search, with what intent and volume. Fix the technical base: indexing, sitemap, page speed, mobile, clean titles and structure, checked in Search Console. Plan content that answers those searches better than the current results, page by page, and link pages together. Earn links with useful content and partners rather than buying them. Track impressions, clicks, positions and conversions monthly: SEO takes months, so set that expectation.

role.q: Which metrics would you put on a weekly marketing dashboard for a manager?
role.why: Shows you choose a few metrics tied to decisions, not every number available.
role.model: A few metrics tied to the goal, each with its target and the trend: spend, leads or sales, cost per lead or acquisition cost, conversion rate, and revenue or pipeline per channel. Then one or two leading indicators, such as qualified traffic and e-mail engagement. Each metric gets a definition so finance and sales read it the same way, and a short written comment on what changed and what we do about it. Detail by campaign goes on a second page.

role.q: How do you run and read an A/B test on a landing page?
role.why: Experiments are how marketers prove impact; recruiters check the basics of method.
role.model: Write a hypothesis with one change and one main metric, for example the sign-up rate. Size the test before starting: from the current rate and the smallest lift worth having, compute the visitors needed, and fix the duration in full weeks. Split traffic randomly and check the split is balanced. Do not stop early when it looks good. At the end, read the difference with its confidence interval, check segments only to learn, and write down the decision and what you will test next.

role.q: How would you split a budget between Google Ads, paid social and SEO?
role.why: Tests whether you reason from goals and data rather than habit.
role.model: It depends on the goal and the funnel stage. Search ads capture existing demand and are easy to measure; paid social creates demand and works for audiences that do not search yet; SEO is slower but cheaper over time. I would start from past results per channel (cost per acquisition and volume), keep most of the budget where returns are proven, and test a smaller share on new channels with clear stop rules. I review the split monthly and watch for diminishing returns when a channel gets more budget.

role.q: Sales says the leads from marketing are bad. What do you do?
role.why: Marketing and sales alignment comes up in every B2B role.
role.model: Agree first on what a qualified lead is, with sales, in writing: the criteria and who follows up and when. Then look at the data in the CRM: lead source, campaign, conversion to meeting and to deal, and follow-up times. Often the issue is in both places: targeting that is too broad, and leads followed up late. Adjust targeting and forms, add lead scoring if volume allows, and share a joint weekly report so both teams look at the same numbers.

role.q: What do you check before sending an e-mail campaign to 50,000 contacts?
role.why: Shows care, compliance and testing habits.
role.model: Consent and the list: only contacts who opted in, unsubscribed and bounced addresses removed, and the segment matches the message (GDPR in Europe). The content: subject line, preview text, personalisation with fallbacks, links and tracking parameters, an easy unsubscribe link, and how it looks on mobile and in dark mode. Deliverability: authenticated sending domain (SPF, DKIM, DMARC). Then a test send to several inboxes, a subject line test on a sample if useful, and the goal metric decided before sending.

role.q: Tell me about a campaign you are proud of.
role.why: They want a structured story with numbers and your own role.
role.model: Use the STAR structure. Situation and goal in one sentence, with a number (for example, lower the cost per lead by 20 % in a quarter). What you did yourself: the analysis, the audience or message you changed, the test you ran. The result with numbers and the time it took, then what you learned and would do differently. If you have no job experience yet, use a personal project or a case study with real data: say so honestly.
